tasks.outcome: Make each built copy of the program carry the version of the code it was built from.

actions.what: Rewrites the generated version file so the program carries the current Git commit description.

rules.statement: When the build script runs, it replaces the program's version in a generated source file with the text git gives for the current commit. That text is a tag, commit count and short commit name when tags exist, and a short commit name otherwise. The script runs when someone runs it or the release workflow does. The committed file holds an empty version.

tasks.outcome: Obtain Microsoft's current set of policy definitions and install them in a folder the program can use.

actions.what: Lets the person pick the destination folder in a folder dialog.
Downloads Microsoft's policy definitions package, unpacks it and moves the files into the chosen folder.
Fills the destination folder with the Windows policy definitions folder and clears the busy state.
Blocks closing the window while a download is running.

rules.statement: Before any file is moved, when the folder written in the destination box already exists and the person is an administrator, ownership of it is taken and Administrators are given full control. This applies to whatever folder text is in the box, not only the Windows folder; a standard user skips it. A failure ends the download with "Failed to take control of the destination." and nothing is moved.

When any step fails, the person is told "Failed to " followed by the step that failed (create a scratch space, download the package, extract the package, take control of the destination, move the ADMX files, remove temporary files); the window stays open, controls are re-enabled, and no policy folder is reported. If only the final cleanup of the scratch folder fails, all files are already installed yet the person is told "Failed to remove temporary files." and no new policy folder is offered.

While a download runs, the start button, close button, destination box and browse button are all disabled, so a second download cannot be started and the destination cannot change; they are enabled again when it ends.

The template files are moved into the destination, then the language files for the person's regional format language (the culture of the regional settings, which can differ from the display language) are moved into a folder of that name if the package holds one. Unless that language is en-US, the English files are also moved into an en-US folder as a fallback; if the package has no en-US folder, the download stops with "Failed to move the ADMX files." after the destination files were already replaced.

When files are moved into a folder, the folder is created if missing and every file already there with the same name is deleted first and then replaced by the new one, with no backup. Only files directly in the source folder are moved. A failure part-way leaves some files replaced and others not.

Each time the download window opens, the destination folder is set to the Windows policy definitions folder (the PolicyDefinitions folder under the Windows folder) and no new policy folder is reported to the caller.

Starting the download always fetches one fixed Microsoft package, the Windows 11 September 2026 Update (26H2) administrative templates, into a scratch folder under the person's local application data as "W11Admx.msi"; the person cannot choose another version.

For an administrator, each folder handed to the file move that already exists, the destination itself and any existing language folder, has its ownership taken; a language folder created during the move instead inherits permissions from the folder above. Every moved file, including the template files in the destination, is reset to inherit permissions. A standard user changes no permissions. A failure here ends the download with "Failed to move the ADMX files.", not the take-control message.
When the person closes the download window while a download is running, the close is refused; the window closes only when no download is running.
Choosing a folder in the browse dialog replaces the destination; cancelling the dialog leaves the destination unchanged.

After a successful download the scratch folder is deleted, the person is asked "ADMX files downloaded successfully. Open them now?", and the destination is reported as the new policy folder only if they answer Yes; either answer closes the window as done.

The downloaded package is unpacked with the Windows installer tool; if the tool ends with a non-zero code the download stops with "Failed to extract the package." and the package is kept. When it succeeds, the downloaded package file is deleted.

tasks.outcome: Be offered the full set of policy definitions the first time the program is used on an edition that lacks them.

actions.what: On first run without a full set of definitions, offers to download them.

rules.statement: A category is orphaned when it has no parent among the loaded definitions although its definition names one.

When the offer is considered, it is made only if this Windows edition has no Group Policy support and more than two non-empty categories name a parent that is not among the loaded definitions. The person sees "Welcome to Policy Plus! Home editions do not come with the full set of policy definitions. Would you like to download them now? This can also be done later with Help | Acquire ADMX Files."; Yes starts the download dialog.

The computer counts as having the Group Policy infrastructure only when the number Windows gives for its edition equals one of 59 fixed codes in a list. The edition is asked for as Windows version 6.0, and the result of the call is not checked. When the call fails the edition stays 0, which is not in the list, so the computer counts as having none.

The welcome offer to download policy definitions is considered only once: the first time the window is shown the program records that it has been considered, even when no offer is made, and never considers it again.
A category is empty when it holds no subcategories and no policies at all, counting hidden ones.

tasks.outcome: Make the newly downloaded policy definitions the ones the program works with.

actions.what: Opens the download window and loads the downloaded definitions.

rules.statement: A category's icon is chosen in this order: orphaned, then empty, then normal.
A name or description written as "$(string.<id>)" shows the language file's text for that id; an unknown id shows the code itself; any other text is shown as written; an empty value stays empty.
For a policy's list elements, a marked-for-deletion list counts as one deleted element, and a list that holds any values counts as a present element and cancels that deletion.
A policy's lists of on-values and off-values count as enabled or disabled evidence for each value in them that is present, using the list's own key when it names one.

A language file's text table is read only from its first text table, and each text is kept under its id; when the same text id appears twice, the file is refused as invalid and its template file is not loaded.
A category is visible when empty categories are switched on. Otherwise it is visible only if it has at least one visible policy or one visible subcategory.

A policy is visible only if it applies to a chosen area (user, computer or both). With "Only Filtered Policies" on, it must also pass the filter for a chosen area it applies to; passing for either one is enough.
A policy shows the 'supported on' rule its reference names, found in this load or earlier ones; when none is found it has none.

With both areas shown, a policy that applies to both areas shows its common state followed by "(2)" when both match, the computer state followed by "(C)" when only the user is Not Configured, the user state followed by "(U)" when only the computer is Not Configured, and "Mixed" otherwise.
A filter on state keeps only policies whose state in the checked area is Configured (Enabled or Disabled), Not Configured, Disabled or Enabled, as chosen.
A category's explanation is optional. A category with any content inside it (even a comment) must contain a parent entry with a reference; otherwise the template is refused as invalid.
When nothing is selected, the title and support lines are hidden and the pane reads "Select an item to see its description.".

A value in a policy file counts as marked for deletion when a deletion marker names it, when the key has a clear-all marker, or when a delete-values list for the key names it, regardless of case. Entries are examined in sorted order, and a value whose name sorts after the marker is stored as present and cancels the deletion, whenever it was written and whichever marker kind came before.
Listing the values of a key in a policy file leaves out the marker entries unless the caller asks for them.
A number box takes default value 1, shows its up-down spinner and steps by 1 unless the language file says otherwise; an unreadable attribute value falls back to the same defaults.
A policy's switched-on and switched-off effects are read from its enabled and disabled values and lists; a list entry names a value and optionally its own key, falling back to the list's default key.

A number option accepts 0 to 4,294,967,295 unless the template sets other limits, overwrites existing values unless marked soft, and is stored as a number unless marked as text; unreadable attribute values fall back to these defaults.
A support rule entry is linked to the product its reference names; when no such product exists it is linked to the support rule of that name; when neither exists it stays unlinked.
A policy takes its category and its 'supported on' rule from the references in its own content, and has options only when it contains an options section.

A category whose parent is named is attached under that parent, found among items of this load or of files loaded earlier; when the parent is not found, the category has no parent but is still listed among the top-level categories.
An XML attribute that is absent gives nothing.

When a template declares no target namespace, loading the folder stops at once with an error: the files after it are not read, nothing is built, and the person sees the error text (a start-up load also discards the workspace).

A policy gets a settings screen layout only when the template names one, the name is written as "$(presentation.<id>)", and the language file holds a layout with that id; in every other case the policy has none.
For any other element (number, text, choice, multi-line text), a value marked for deletion counts as a deleted element and a value that is present counts as a present element.

A registry key counts as a policy key when it is one of the three policy branches (software\policies, software\microsoft\windows\currentversion\policies, system\currentcontrolset\policies) or lies below one, regardless of case.

A reference containing a colon uses the namespace the template declared for its prefix; with an unknown prefix it is taken as already complete; a reference without a colon belongs to the template's own namespace.
A check box starts unticked unless the language file marks it ticked.
The live registry never reports a value as marked for deletion.

A policy with a registry value of its own counts as enabled evidence when that value holds its 'on' value, which is the number 1 when the template gives none, and as disabled evidence when it holds its 'off' value or is marked for deletion when the template gives none.
Reading a value from a policy file gives nothing when the value is absent or marked for deletion.
A value in the live registry counts as present when its key exists and, unless the value name is empty, the key lists a value of that name, regardless of case. An empty name means the key itself.
A policy option of any kind other than number, yes/no, text, list, choice or multi-line text is dropped without notice.
A category appears in the tree only when it passes the visibility rule; each shown category gets an icon by its kind and carries its visible subcategories below it, and the tree is sorted.
When the chosen language file cannot be parsed as XML, the template is refused with "The ADML XML couldn't be parsed: <detail>"; any other read problem gives "The ADML is invalid: <detail>".
If any element is present, the elements add their count to the enabled evidence; only when none is present do deleted elements add to the disabled evidence.

When loading definitions reports no problems nothing is shown; otherwise the person sees "Errors were encountered while adding administrative templates to the workspace." with each problem, and, only where a choice is wanted, is asked "Continue trying to use this workspace?".

A support definition met a second time anywhere in one evaluation counts as not met, because the list of definitions seen is never emptied. Two entries that point at the same definition, with no cycle, make the second one not met.
A yes/no option takes its registry effect for true and false from true and false values and lists.
With both areas shown, the comment column is empty when neither area has a comment, shows "(multiple)" when both have one, and otherwise shows the single comment.
A text option allows 255 characters, is optional, is stored as plain text and overwrites existing values unless the template says otherwise; unreadable attribute values fall back to these defaults.
A policy is listed under the category its reference names, found in this load or earlier ones; when that category is not found the policy is kept in the policy list but belongs to no category.
A policy's comment in one area is empty when that source has no comment file or holds no comment for the policy, and otherwise the saved text.

When a template file cannot be parsed as XML, it is refused with the message "Couldn't load <path>: The ADMX XML couldn't be parsed: <detail>."; any other read problem is refused with "The ADMX is invalid: <detail>".
A drop-down list has a preselected item only when the language file names one; otherwise none is preselected.
Products form three levels: a product, its major versions and their minor versions; deeper levels are not read, and each version must carry a version index or the file is refused as invalid.

Only labels, number boxes, text boxes, check boxes, combo boxes, drop-down lists, list boxes and multi-line text boxes are kept in a screen layout; any other control in the language file is dropped without notice.

When the structures are built, all new categories, products, support rules and policies join the final lists and the staged items are cleared, so loading further files adds to what is already available.
A value in a policy file counts as present only if it is stored and not marked for deletion.

A choice option is optional unless marked required. Each choice keeps whichever of a single registry value and a list of values it contains, both when both are present; a choice with neither is accepted and changes nothing.
A policy's state in one area reads "Enabled", "Disabled", "Not Configured" or "Unknown"; the computer source is read for the computer area and the user source for any other.
A registry value in a template is a delete marker, a number or a text, decided by the first of those it contains; a value with none of them is treated as a delete marker.
Entries of a combo box or drop-down list are sorted unless the language file says not to sort them.

A support entry for a product that has versions beneath it, whether a version range or a plain entry for a parent product that is not itself chosen, counts as met when any version in its range, or a sub-product directly beneath one, is chosen. The range runs from the entry's minimum (0 if none) to its maximum (the highest version if none). A range entry never matches on its own product, and a product with no versions beneath it never matches this way.

An option's registry value name is taken from its own value name, except for a list option that has a value prefix attribute: the prefix is used and the own value name only when that prefix is empty. A list option counts as prefixed whenever the attribute is present, even if empty.

When the caller asks for 'any' matching, a support definition whose logic is all-of needs every entry met, and any other definition needs one entry met. When the caller does not ask for 'any', every definition, all-of included, is met by one entry. A definition with no entries, or none met, is met only when all are required. Plain product entries are checked before nested definitions.
The category tree selection follows the category shown in the right pane.

The right pane lists the chosen category in this order: an "Up: <parent name>" row marked "Parent" when the category has a parent, then visible subcategories by name, then visible policies by name. Each policy row shows its state and its comment text.

For a selected or highlighted category the pane shows its title, "This category contains N policies and M subcategories." ("The selected category" when highlighted but not opened) and its explanation. The counts include every policy and subcategory, hidden or not.

A value counts as present when: for a deletion marker, it is marked for deletion; for a number, it exists as a whole number and equals the expected number; for text, it exists as text and equals the expected text. A value of the wrong kind is not present.
The text of a policy description is tidied for display: leading and trailing spaces are removed from every line and blank space at the end of the text is dropped.
An item's unique name is its template's namespace, a colon and its own name, so equal names in different templates stay apart.

A list option replaces other entries of its key unless marked additive, stores plain text unless marked expandable, numbers entries automatically unless the template says the person names them, and counts as prefixed only when a value prefix is given.
A control keeps the reference id the language file gives it, which ties it to the matching setting option in the template file; a control without one has no id.
A child product (major or minor version) is attached under its parent product, which must be defined in the same template file; only products without a parent are listed as top-level products.
A filter on managed policies hides preferences when managed policies are wanted, and hides managed policies when preferences are wanted.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for checking whether a value will be deleted: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.
A policy applies to computers when its class is "Machine", to users when "User", and to both for any other class value.

When the list is rebuilt, the policy already selected is selected again and revealed only if it is still listed, that is, it sits in the category shown and passes the visibility rule; otherwise nothing is selected. Then, if the policy is in the same category and the list still has that many rows, the earlier top row is put back, so the policy is not guaranteed to stay in view.
When no language file is found in any of those places, the template file is refused with "The corresponding ADML is missing" and none of its content is loaded.
A policy passes the filter only when it passes every active part of it.

When a template file is refused with a reported failure (unparsable, invalid, namespace already owned, or no usable language file), it is skipped and the failure is listed; the other files in the folder still load and the structures are built from those that loaded.
Text read from a policy file stops at its first empty character, and a multiple-string value ends at its first empty string.

For a checkbox element: a value marked for deletion counts as one deleted element. Otherwise, each present off value (or off-list value) counts a tenth of a deleted element, and each present on value (or on-list value) counts one present element. A checkbox whose template declares no on value or on list adds no present evidence, even if it holds 1.
Closing the workspace or replacing it with a new one discards all loaded definitions and the previous search results.

For a selected policy the information pane shows its title, "(no requirements information)" when it has no support rule or "Requirements:" plus the support name, and its explanation. A notice that the policy is a preference appears only for preferences.
A policy's icon is chosen in this order: preference, then plain when it has no configurable elements, then "extra configuration" when it has some.
A policy applies to an area when its definition declares that area; a policy declared for both applies to each.
A filter on comments keeps only policies that have a non-empty comment in the checked area, or only those that have none, as chosen.

When a template file's namespace is already held by a template file loaded earlier, it is refused with "The <namespace> namespace is already owned by a different ADMX file", so the same file cannot be added twice.
When a policy lists no supported-on information, it counts as supported only if the caller allows unlisted policies. The same applies to a support entry that names no known product.

A template's superseded-ADM file name and minimum language revision are read when present; a superseded entry without a file name, or a minimum revision that is missing or not a number, refuses the template as invalid.
A language file's screen layouts are read only from its first presentation table; when the same layout id appears twice, the file is refused as invalid and its template file is not loaded.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for reading a value: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.
Only files directly in the chosen folder whose names end in .admx (in any letter case) are loaded as templates; subfolders and other files are ignored.
An XML attribute that is absent, or whose text is not valid for the type of the stated default, gives that default.

With both areas shown, a policy that applies to one area shows that area's state followed by "(C)" for computer or "(U)" for user. With a single area shown, only that area's state is shown, without a suffix.
A stored policy file value is read back as text for text and expandable text, a 32-bit or 64-bit number for numbers, a list of strings for multiple strings, and raw bytes for every other type.

When both a template file and its language file load, the template's categories, products, support rules and policies are staged for the next build and the pair is recorded as loaded under the template's namespace.
The namespace of a template is the one listed as its target; each prefix a template declares must be unique, and a repeated prefix refuses the file as invalid.

The language file for a template is taken from the subfolder named exactly by the language code if it holds this template's file; else from the first subfolder whose name starts with the same language part (before the dash, compared with capital letters mattering) that holds this template's file; else from the en-US subfolder if it holds it. A folder lacking the file is skipped.

A policy is Enabled when enabled evidence exceeds disabled evidence, Disabled when disabled exceeds enabled, Not configured when there is no evidence either way, and Unclear when both are equal and above zero.
The language for definition text is the saved language code, or the computer's own language when none is saved.
When a language file has no policy resources section, or its revision is missing or not a number, the file is refused as invalid and its template file is not loaded.

A policy is a preference, not a managed policy, when it names a registry key outside the three policy locations: software\policies, software\microsoft\windows\currentversion\policies and system\currentcontrolset\policies.
After a successful download of definitions, the workspace is emptied, the downloaded folder loaded and saved as the definitions folder, and the view rebuilt; with no new folder nothing changes.
After the category tree is rebuilt from the loaded definitions, no category, policy or highlighted item is selected and the information pane shows the empty state.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for listing a key's values: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.
Reading a value from the live registry gives nothing when the key is missing. Signed numbers are returned as the unsigned numbers policies use, and environment variables in text are not expanded.

A support rule is 'any of' when its first logic element is "or", 'all of' when it is "and", and blank otherwise; only that first logic element is read, each reference or range in it becomes an entry, and a range may carry a minimum and maximum version.
Clearing the search forgets the results, so reopening them reports that no search has been run.
A filter on products keeps only policies supported by the chosen products, honouring the options to match any product and to include policies with blank support.

A template file is refused as invalid when any of these is missing or unreadable: the policy definitions section; a namespace entry's prefix or namespace; a superseded-ADM file name; a minimum revision (missing or not a number); a support rule's name or display name; a support reference or range without its reference, or a version bound that is not a whole number; a product's name, display name or version index; a category's name or display name; a category's parent entry or its reference when the category has content; a policy's name, display name, key or class; a policy's category or supported-on reference; a number value's value; a list item's value name; a choice item's display name; or an option's id.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for asking whether a value is present: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.

A support entry for a product counts as met in two cases. The entry is not a version range and that exact product is among the chosen products. Or the product has versions beneath it, and any of those versions or their sub-products is chosen, even when the product itself is not.

tasks.outcome: Get back to the policy work where it was left: the last policy sources and policy definitions are ready to browse.

actions.what: Starts the program: restores the last definitions folder and policy sources, then fills the category tree.

rules.statement: A Scratch space source is an empty policy store that can be changed but is never saved anywhere.
The program allows secure connections using TLS 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2 only, so downloads use no other protocol.

When the program's settings area in the registry cannot be opened or created, the program carries on without it: settings read as their defaults, changes are dropped, and the person is not told, so settings are not remembered between runs.
On first start, when no policy sources were saved, both the user source and the computer source open as the local Group Policy files (Local GPO) with no extra location.
The source name shown in the status bar is Local GPO, Registry, File, User GPO, User hive or Scratch space, followed by the path or SID in brackets when there is one.

No comment of a comment file can be read when any comment's policy reference has no colon or a prefix that is not declared, its text is not written as "$(resource.<id>)", its text id is missing, or two comments resolve to the same policy.
When a number is saved to the live registry, an unsigned 32-bit or 64-bit number is converted to the signed number the registry stores with the same bits, and the key is created if missing.
A registry source counts as writable only when a test value can be written under Software\Policies and removed again; otherwise it is read-only.
A policy file is refused when its format version is not 1, with the message 'Unknown (newer) version of POL format'.
The definitions folder to load is the one saved last time; when none is saved it is the Windows PolicyDefinitions folder.

When loading the saved definitions reports problems, the person is asked whether to keep using the workspace. Yes keeps the partly loaded workspace. No raises the failure "You decided to not use the problematic ADMX bundle.", which goes into the failed-load handling: the workspace is thrown away, and for a non-default folder the person is asked to load the default, while for the default folder the person is told the definitions could not be loaded.

A source read through the file branch covers a POL file, the local Group Policy and a per-user Group Policy, each with a Registry.pol path. An existing file is loaded; it is writable only when it can be opened for reading and writing, otherwise it can be viewed but not committed.

A user hive source is mounted by loading the hive file under a fresh temporary name in the machine registry, after the backup and restore privileges are switched on. If the hive cannot be opened afterwards, the source becomes an empty, read-only scratch source instead, without telling the person.

A registry source must start with HKCU, HKEY_CURRENT_USER, HKU, HKEY_USERS, HKLM or HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (any case); otherwise it is refused with "The root key is not valid." A path after the root is opened, and created if missing.

When a policy file is read and the same key and value name occur twice, the later entry wins. Key and value names are matched without regard to letter case, and the first spelling seen is kept for saving.
When the person chooses to load the default location, the workspace is replaced by an empty one and the Windows default folder is loaded into it.

The comment file for a source sits beside its file: the POL file or hive path with the extension changed to .cmtx; for Local GPO or per-user GPO a file named comment.cmtx in the same folder; for the registry a file under the person's local application data folder (one for user, one for machine); Scratch space has none, so comments are unavailable.
A policy file is refused when it does not start with the 'PReg' signature, with the message 'Missing PReg signature'.
When the Windows default folder itself fails to load, or fails to load after the person chose Yes, the person is told "Policy definitions could not be loaded: <reason>" and the workspace stays empty.

When the policy sources dialog opens with the last-used sources, each side is set to the remembered kind (Local GPO, Registry, POL file, Scratch space, and for users also per-user GPO or user hive), and the registry path, file name, SID or hive path is filled in only for the kinds that carry one.
A policy source's writability is described as "is fully writable", "cannot be saved" (changes work in memory only) or "cannot be modified"; anything but fully writable counts as a problem.

The path of a policy source is fixed by its kind: Local GPO uses the Registry.pol file of the system's local Group Policy (user or machine folder) and its gpt.ini; a per-user GPO uses the folder named by the person's SID under GroupPolicyUsers; a POL file and a user hive use the path given; Scratch space has none.
When a policy file is read, an extra empty character after the value name, as Microsoft's documentation allows, is skipped.

A source's comments are used only when it has a comment file location. The folder is created if missing; an existing file is loaded and a missing file gives no comments yet. Any failure leaves that source without comments.
When a policy file is saved, entries are written in alphabetical order, so a key-clearing marker is always written before the values it clears.

When the saved folder is not the Windows default and fails to load, the person is told "Policy definitions could not be loaded from "<folder>": <reason> Load from the default location?". Yes saves the Windows default folder as the definitions folder; No leaves the workspace empty with no further message.

When the Registry.pol of a POL file source, the local Group Policy or a per-user Group Policy does not exist, it is created empty with its folder and treated as writable; a mistyped SID therefore creates a new folder and empty file under the per-user policy folder. If creation fails, an empty read-only source is used and no error is shown.

When the previously saved policy sources cannot be opened, the person is told "The previous policy sources are not accessible. The defaults will be loaded." and both sources are saved as Local GPO, then opened quietly. Only the source type is reset; any saved location text stays.

Opening new policy sources first closes the ones already open. Unsaved changes are discarded for sources backed by a POL file (local Group Policy files, a chosen POL file, a per-user Group Policy object) and for the empty source. A registry source applies changes at once, and a user hive file is applied when it is closed, so those lose nothing.

A source is writable by default for Scratch space; for a registry source it is 'no writing' when the write test failed; for others it is 'no commit' when the file or hive could not be opened for writing.
The list of areas starts on "User or Computer", the first choice, so both user and computer policies are shown at start.

A comment file is refused as unreadable when it has no comment-definitions section, a namespace entry without a prefix, a comment without a policy reference, a text without an id, or a repeated prefix, policy reference or text id. The comments of that source are then unavailable.
When a value is deleted in the live registry and its key does not exist, nothing happens. A missing value is not an error.

After opening, if either source is not fully writable the person is told "Not all policy sources are fully writable." with the state of the user and the computer source; if both are fully writable, "Both the user and computer policy sources are loaded and writable." appears only when opening was not quiet (never at start).

tasks.outcome: Choose the language in which policy definition text is shown and have it applied.

actions.what: Chooses the language of the definition text and offers to reload the workspace.
Validates the language code and returns it, or cancels when unchanged.

rules.statement: When the person confirms the language dialog with text that does not split into exactly two parts around a hyphen (for example "en" or "en-US-x"), it is refused with "Please enter a valid language code." and stays open. Any text with exactly one hyphen passes, including "-", "en-" or text with path characters: it is not checked as a real language code. The code is later used as a folder name when looking for ADML files.

Setting the language saves the new language code at once, then asks "Language changes will take effect when ADML files are next loaded. Would you like to reload the workspace now?". Yes empties the workspace and reloads the saved definitions folder.

actions.what: Saves comments and policy settings to their sources and remembers the chosen sources.

rules.statement: When gpt.ini does not exist, a new one is written with the General section, both extension-name lines and Version 65537.

When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry is saved only if it has a non-empty value name that does not start with '**'. Other marker-style entries and entries with an empty value name are skipped without notice. A saved value keeps its original letter case and type.
When gpt.ini is updated and already exists, its Version number is raised by 1 for a machine source and by 65536 for a user source; if no Version line exists, it is set to 65537 (both parts at 1).
When a policy file is clearing a key, all values and markers under the key are dropped and a single clear-all marker is stored.

Saving writes each source's comments first, then writes a source only if it is fully writable (otherwise reported as "not writable"), then remembers the chosen source types and locations for the next start. The person sees "Success." with the user and computer outcomes, or "Saving failed!" with the reason.

A REG file cannot be used as a source for forgetting a value: the request fails with 'not implemented'. Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a REG file fails this way for any dropped value under a policy branch.

Saving a local Group Policy source writes the Registry.pol file, raises the gpt.ini version, and then, on Windows editions that list as having Group Policy (decided by a fixed list of product edition codes), asks Windows to refresh policy ("saved to disk and invoked policy refresh"). On other editions, the difference between the file as last on disk (read at the moment of saving) and the new content is applied to the running account's own registry (the current user's for a user source, the machine's for a machine source) and all windows are notified ("saved to disk and applied diff to Registry").
Saving a per-user GPO writes its Registry.pol file, raises its gpt.ini version and asks Windows to refresh user policy ("saved to disk and invoked policy refresh").

When a value is saved into a REG file, it is ignored if a source branch is set and its key lies outside that branch. When no branch is set, every key is accepted. Any value already stored under that name is replaced.

Saving a POL file source writes the file only ("saved to disk"); a registry source reports "already applied" because it was changed live; a user hive reports "will apply when policy source is closed"; Scratch space reports "discarded".

When a value is deleted in a REG file, the request is ignored if a source branch is set and the key lies outside it, or if the key is already marked for removal. When no branch is set, every key is accepted. Otherwise the value is recorded as deleted.
When gpt.ini is updated, the Machine and User extension-name lines for the registry policy are added if missing and left untouched if present.

When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry starting '**deletekeys' clears each key named in its semicolon-separated list under the entry's key, using lower-case names. Clearing removes only that key's own values, not its subkeys.

When comments are saved, each comment gets its own text id built from the policy's namespace, policy name and a running number, and each distinct namespace gets a prefix made from its name (dots turned into underscores) and the running number.

When a newer policy file is applied over an older one, values the old file held and the new one dropped are forgotten in the target, but only if they sit under the three policy branches of the registry.
In the live registry, 'forgetting' a value deletes it, because the registry cannot remember a pending deletion.
When a value is forgotten in a policy file, both the value and its deletion marker are removed, so the policy reverts to not saying anything about it.
Clearing a key in the live registry deletes every value in it but leaves the key and its subkeys. Forgetting a key's clearance does nothing.
A multiple-string value is stored as its strings each followed by an empty character, with one more empty character closing the list.
A 64-bit number is stored in a policy file as 8 bytes, lowest byte first.
Saving comments writes every comment and text held in memory into the target file, in schema version 1.0, replacing what the file held before.

When a key is cleared in a REG file, the request is ignored if a source branch is set and the key lies outside it. When no branch is set, every key is accepted. Otherwise the key's earlier entries are replaced by a key-removal entry.
When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry named '**deletevalues' deletes each value in its semicolon-separated list, using lower-case names.
A 32-bit number is stored in a policy file as 4 bytes, lowest byte first.

When a value is marked for deletion in a policy file, any value or marker already held under that name is dropped first. A deletion marker holding the number 32, as Microsoft does, is added unless the value is already marked or its key is cleared.
When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry named '**del.' plus a value name deletes that value, using the lower-case key and value names.
When a value is set in a policy file, it replaces any value already held under that name. A deletion marker for the name is not removed.
A source's comment list is saved to its comment file location whenever the list exists, even when empty; a source without comment support has no list and is skipped.
Text stored in a policy file is written in two-byte characters followed by a closing empty character.

When a policy file's changes are applied to another source, an entry starting '**delvals' clears the whole key, using the lower-case key name. Entries are applied in sorted order, so clear-all entries come before values. Clearing a live registry key removes only that key's own values.
A value written to a policy file is stored as text, expandable text, a 32-bit or 64-bit number or a multiple string by its stated type. Every other type is stored as raw bytes with that type.

rules.statement: The comment box is disabled and reads "Comments unavailable for this policy source" when the source has no comments; otherwise it shows the policy's stored comment, or is empty when there is none.
When a policy is set to Disabled and the definition gives no off value, its registry value is removed. A defined off value, with any extra off values, is saved instead.

A choice element is read as the position of the first item whose own value is present and, when the item has a value list, whose list is wholly present; when no item matches, the position is -1.
When a policy is forgotten, the whole key of each of its list elements is cleared and every registry value it touches is dropped from the source, so it reads as Not configured.
The state shown when the dialog opens follows the policy's present state in the source being edited: Enabled, Disabled, or Not Configured for anything else, including an unclear state.
When a policy is applied and the source supports comments, an empty comment box removes the policy's stored comment and any text replaces or adds it.
A list element whose entries have names the person provides is read as every stored name with its value, under the element's key.

Remove or rename all but one." and nothing is returned. Names are compared exactly, so Run and run are accepted as two entries. A name cell never filled in stops the dialog with an unhandled error.
A list of values counts as present only when every value in it is present.
OK writes the policy to the source and closes the dialog as a change.
The saved value of a multi-line text element is read as stored, without first checking that it exists.

When a list setting is saved, entries that carry their own names are saved under those names. Otherwise each entry is numbered from 1, named with the definition's prefix plus its number, or named after its own text when the definition has no prefix.
A check box starts with the presentation's default state.

Choosing Computer or User in the dialog switches the source, its writability and its comments to that section, and reloads the chosen state (Enabled, Disabled or Not Configured) from it. Option values are replaced only for options the section stores when it is Enabled; other values typed earlier stay in the controls.
A plain text entry is limited to the maximum length the policy defines and starts with the presentation's default text.
A checkbox is on when its on value (or all values of its on list) is present, or, with neither defined, when its value is 1; it is off in every other case, including when its off value is present.

When a key's clearance is forgotten in a REG file, the key-removal entry is dropped if it exists. The request is ignored if a source branch is set and the key lies outside it. When no branch is set, every key is accepted.

The registry values a policy touches are its own value, those in its value lists, those of its elements (the whole key for list elements) and those of checkbox and choice sub-lists, each counted once.
A setting that names its own registry key is saved under that key. Otherwise it is saved under the policy's key.
Apply writes the policy to the source, keeps the dialog open and records that a change was made.
When a multi-line text setting is saved, it is written as a multiple-string value.

When a policy is set to Disabled, each setting gets only its own removal. A list setting has all values under its key removed, even when its definition says to keep other entries. A checkbox with a defined off value or off list gets those saved, and every other setting has its single value removed. Extra values listed for a chosen item, a checkbox's on list and the policy's own on list are left in place.
Option controls can be edited only while Enabled is chosen; with Disabled or Not Configured they are greyed out.
When a key's clearance is forgotten in a policy file, every clear-all marker for that key is removed.
When Enabled is chosen, applying writes every option of the policy whatever its value, including options never filled in.
When a text setting is saved, it is written as an expandable text string if the definition says so, otherwise as a plain text string.
Closing the policy setting dialog with Cancel is reported as a change when Apply was used earlier in that session, and as a cancel otherwise.
When a policy is set to Enabled, its own on value is saved and any extra values listed for the on state are saved with it. A key left blank in a list falls back to the policy's key.

When a checkbox setting is saved, a ticked box with no defined on value first saves the number 1, and an unticked box with no defined off value first removes the value. The defined on or off value is then saved, with the extra values listed for that state, and overwrites the first step.

When the list editor is confirmed for a list without names, every row except the empty new row at the bottom is returned in the order shown, with no check that a cell has content; a row whose value cell was never filled is returned as an empty entry. For named lists the same new row is ignored.
When a list setting is saved and the definition does not say to keep other entries, every existing value under the list's key is removed first. A list with no supplied entries then stays empty.

A plain number box keeps any text a whole-number reading accepts, including a leading sign or spaces; other text is replaced by the default. A number above the maximum or below the minimum is replaced by that limit. Numbers above 2,147,483,647 are replaced by the default even when the policy maximum is higher. Only typing is restricted to digits; pasted text is not. A negative number kept where the minimum is below zero is converted to an unsigned number when applied.
A number entered with a spin box is limited to the minimum and maximum the policy defines, in steps the presentation sets, and starts at the presentation's default.

When a registry value is written for a policy, a value defined as 'delete' is removed, a numeric value is saved as a 32-bit number and a text value as a text string. A policy with no value defined writes nothing.

Applying a policy first forgets everything the source holds for it; Enabled then writes every option's current value, Disabled writes the disabled state, and Not Configured leaves the policy with no values.
When a policy is set to Not configured or Unknown, SetPolicyState writes and removes nothing. Callers forget the policy's old values first, so Not configured works by that removal alone.

When the policy is Enabled, each option control is set to the value found in the source: numbers into number boxes, text into text and combo boxes, the matching item in drop-downs, true or false into check boxes, lines into multi-line boxes and the stored list into the list editor.

A list element whose entry names do not matter is read as a list of values: when the list has a prefix, the stored values named prefix1, prefix2, and so on, in order, until the first number that is missing; otherwise every stored value name under the key.

When a choice setting is saved, the value of the chosen item is saved together with any extra values that item lists. When the chosen position does not exist, the code fails at that point: values already written for earlier settings of the same policy stay written and nothing undoes them, so the policy is left half set.
The saved value of a number or text element is read as stored; the reading assumes the value exists and is of the right kind, and is not checked first. A checkbox is read by its own rule.

A drop-down list shows the policy's choices by their translated names, sorted unless the presentation turns sorting off, and preselects the default choice when the presentation names one; otherwise nothing is selected.
When a policy is set to Enabled, only the settings the person supplied are written. A setting with no supplied value is left as it was.

A text entry with suggestions is limited to the maximum length the policy defines, starts with the presentation's default text, and lists the presentation's suggestions, sorted unless the presentation turns sorting off.

When a semantic policy is applied, the policy's earlier settings are wiped first and then the stated state and settings are written.
Verify reads the SPOL text and reports "Validation successful, N policy settings found." or "SPOL validation failed: " followed by the reason; nothing is applied.
A comment line in a semantic policy script is recognised without regard to letter case. A backslash followed by another backslash is one backslash, and a backslash followed by 'n' is a line break.

A setting value in a semantic policy script is read in this order. Starting with # is a whole number, and a # value that is not a whole number fails with a conversion message. A plain non-negative number is an unsigned number. 'True' or 'False', in any letter case, is a yes/no value. Text in single quotes is text, and text in double quotes is a list of text. 'None' is an empty list. Anything else is refused with 'Unknown option data format.'.

Open File puts the whole chosen file into the text box, replacing what was typed without asking and without checking it; Reset, after a Yes to "Are you sure you want to reset the text box?", restores the header "Policy Plus Semantic Policy" and blank lines.
Apply accepts only SPOL text that reads correctly; the parsed file is passed back to the main window. Invalid text is refused with "The SPOL text is invalid: " and the reason.
A semantic policy script is refused unless its first line is 'Policy Plus Semantic Policy', with the message 'Incorrect signature.'.
The state in a semantic policy script must be 'Not configured', 'Enabled' or 'Disabled', regardless of case. Anything else is refused with 'Unknown policy state.'.

When a semantic policy script is applied to many policies, a policy that fails is skipped and counted, and the rest are still applied. The caller gets only the number of failures, not which policy or why.
A semantic policy script applies each policy to the machine source or the user source by its section.
When a semantic policy script fails to load, the error gives the line it stopped at, in the form '(Error found on line N.)'.
Opening Import SPOL discards any previously parsed SPOL so a cancelled session passes nothing back.
A semantic policy script is read in lines separated by carriage return and line feed. A script using line feeds alone is read as one line, so it is refused with the signature message.

Importing semantic policy applies all its policies to both sources and comments; the person sees "Semantic Policy successfully applied." or "N out of M could not be applied." when some failed, and the view refreshes either way.

A comment in a semantic policy script is refused when it ends with a lone backslash, with the message 'Escape sequence started at end of comment.'. A backslash followed by any other character is refused with 'Unknown comment escape sequence' naming it.

A policy header line in a semantic policy script is a user policy only when its first word is exactly 'U'. Any other first word, including lowercase 'u' or 'User', is a machine policy. A bracketed setting in a semantic policy script holds one line per entry. Entries with one text are a list, entries with two texts are a table of name and value. When the results window is reopened, the previously selected result is selected again if it is still in the list.
Find Next moves to the next result that is currently visible, skipping hidden ones, and tells the person "There are no more results that match the filter." when none is left.
Starting a search clears earlier results, sets the progress range to the number of policies, and begins on "Starting search".

When search results are opened from the main window and no search has been run (or it was cleared), the person is told "No search has been run yet, so there are no results to display." and nothing opens.
Go, or a double-click on a result, accepts only when a result is selected; the selected policy is passed back and its position remembered.
Taking the next policy returns nothing when no search has run or when the last result has been passed; otherwise it returns the result after the last chosen one.
When a search ends it reports "Finished searching: checked N policies, found M hits", or "Search canceled: ..." if stopped, and the Stop button is disabled.
"Search Results" only reopens the last results and starts no new search.
The search tests every policy in turn, and adds every hit to the list with its category name, in the order policies are held.
A search dialog opens either empty or running a new search. When the person picks a result, its editor opens in the current area and the list moves to that policy.
The list and progress are refreshed after every 20 policies: "Searching: checked N policies so far, found M hits".

tasks.outcome: Limit the policy list to policies of a chosen type, state, comment status and supported products, and switch that limit on or off.

actions.what: Closes the dialog as cancelled when Escape is pressed
Enables the product requirements box only while Supported on is ticked
Sets the dialog back to a filter that matches everything
Switches whether the filter is applied to the lists.
Applies the new tick to all child products
Drops the double-click message so the tree check state stays in step
Asks for filter settings and turns the filtered view on.
Recolours the product tree so it looks right when disabled
Builds the filter from the chosen options and closes the dialog accepted

rules.statement: When the current filter has a supported-on condition, the dialog opens with Supported on ticked, exactly the filter's products ticked and the two matching options set as the filter holds; product branches whose tick differs from their parent are opened.
When OK is pressed, the new filter keeps only managed policies for Policy, only unmanaged ones for Preference, and no policy-type condition for Any.
When the filter dialog opens, the Current state choice shows Any if the current filter has no state condition, otherwise Not Configured, Configured, Enabled or Disabled as the filter holds.

When the filter dialog opens, the Policy type choice shows Any if the current filter has no policy-type condition, Policy if it keeps only managed policies, and Preference if it keeps only the others.
The "Only Filtered Policies" menu switches the filter on or off and moves to the nearest visible category.
Pressing Escape closes the filter dialog as cancelled and the current filter is unchanged.
Double-clicking a product checkbox does nothing, so a tick shown always agrees with the tick kept.
When the filter dialog opens, the Commented choice shows Any if the current filter has no comment condition, Yes if it keeps only commented policies and No if it keeps only uncommented ones.
Ticking or unticking a product by hand ticks or unticks every product beneath it to match; changes made by the dialog itself do not spread.
When OK is pressed, the new filter keeps only commented policies for Yes, only uncommented ones for No, and no comment condition for Any.

When the current filter has no supported-on condition, the dialog opens with Supported on unticked, both "Match a policy if at least one selected product is supported" and "Match policies with missing or blank support definitions" ticked, and no product ticked.
When OK is pressed, the new filter requires the chosen state: Not Configured, Configured, Enabled or Disabled; Any sets no state condition.
Reset returns every choice to its default: Any for type, state and comment, Supported on unticked, both matching options ticked and no product ticked.
Changing the filter options turns on "Only Filtered Policies" and moves to the nearest visible category.
The product requirement box (the product tree and the two matching options) can be used only while Supported on is ticked; it starts unusable.

When OK is pressed with Supported on ticked, the filter records every ticked product and both matching options; with it unticked, any ticks and options are discarded and no support condition applies. A filter with Supported on ticked and no product ticked is accepted.

tasks.outcome: Open a policy file for direct editing of its raw keys and values, with a warning the first time, and leave the editor when done.

actions.what: After a warning, opens the raw editor on a POL-backed policy source.
Closes the dialog as cancelled when Escape is pressed
Turns the editor buttons on or off to match the kind of item selected in the list.
Closes the editor window with an OK result; the changes were already applied to the policy source as each was made.
Reports the chosen section (user or computer) and closes the dialog as accepted
Closes the editor window with a Cancel result when Escape is pressed; edits already made stay applied to the policy source.

rules.statement: When nothing is selected in the policy file's list, only Add key and Export are available; Add value, Delete value, Edit and Forget are unavailable.
The section dialog lets a person choose only the sections the caller allows: User and Computer are each usable only when enabled by the caller.

Pressing Done (or Enter) closes the raw policy editor as accepted, and pressing Escape closes it as cancelled; there is no Cancel button. The caller ignores the answer, so every change made in the editor stays on the loaded policy source either way, to reach disk only when policies are saved.
Pressing Escape closes the section dialog as cancelled.

When a value is selected in the list, only Forget is always available; Add key, Add value and Export are unavailable, and Edit and Delete value are available only when the value is not already a delete marker.

Raw POL editing is available only when the user or computer source is backed by a POL file, otherwise the person is told "Neither loaded source is backed by a POL file."; the area chosen is limited to POL-backed sources.

Special deletion entries in a policy file are listed as such: "**deletevalues" as "Delete values" with its data, "**del.<name>" as "Delete value" with the name, and entries starting "**delvals" as "Delete all values". They cannot be edited or deleted.

Ordinary values are listed with their content: lists of text joined by spaces, text as it is, 32-bit and 64-bit numbers in decimal, binary data as hexadecimal bytes separated by spaces. Other kinds show no content.
In the section dialog, OK does nothing until User or Computer is chosen; then it returns that section and closes.
A key name in a policy file is listed as a subkey only once, regardless of case, and the requested key itself is never listed.

The raw policy file editor lists keys in alphabetical order ignoring case, each followed by its sub-keys indented, then its values in alphabetical order; a value with an empty name (the marker that keeps an empty key) is not listed.
When a key is selected in the list, Add key, Add value, Delete value, Forget and Export are available, and Edit is unavailable.

The first time raw POL editing is used, the person must accept "Caution! This tool is for very advanced users. Improper modifications may result in inconsistencies in policies' states." (Yes continues and records the acceptance; No cancels and asks again next time).

tasks.outcome: Add a new key, or a new value of a chosen kind, to a policy file.

actions.what: Closes the new value dialog as cancelled when Escape is pressed.
Closes the key name dialog as cancelled when Escape is pressed.
Asks for a new key name, checks it is valid and free, and adds the empty key to the policy file.
Puts the cursor in the key name box with its text selected when the dialog appears.
Asks for a value name and type, then its data, and adds the value under the selected key.

rules.statement: A number entered for a registry value is limited to 0 to 4,294,967,295 for a 32-bit value and to 0 to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 for a 64-bit value.
When the key name dialog is confirmed, the typed name is returned unchecked; when it is cancelled, an empty name is returned, so an empty typed name and a cancel look the same to the caller.
A new key name is refused with "The key name is already taken." when a key of that name, ignoring case, already exists under the same parent.

Adding a value to the selected key lets the person choose a name and one of five kinds; the starting data is empty text, zero, or an empty list by kind, and the value is stored only if the person then confirms its data. A value of the same name in that key is replaced without warning.
A new key name is refused with "The key name is not valid." when it contains a backslash.

Editing a value offers a text, number or list-of-text dialog by kind: text kinds (plain and expandable) a text box, 32-bit and 64-bit numbers a number box, lists of text a multi-line box. Any other kind, such as binary, is refused with "This value kind is not supported." and nothing changes. Cancelling the dialog leaves the value as it was.

The new registry value dialog offers the types String, Expandable string, List of strings, 32-bit DWord and 64-bit QWord, and starts on String. Confirming returns the typed name, unchecked and possibly empty, with the chosen type; cancelling returns neither.

Adding a key does nothing when the name is left empty or the dialog is cancelled; otherwise the key is created under the selected key, or at the top level when nothing is selected, as an empty key, and is selected in the list.

tasks.outcome: Change the data of an existing value in a policy file.

actions.what: Asks for new data for the selected value and stores it in the policy file.
Reads typed hexadecimal text into the value in hexadecimal mode, otherwise leaves it to the standard control.
Switches the number box between decimal and hexadecimal display.
Closes the number dialog as cancelled when Escape is pressed.
Closes the list-of-strings dialog as cancelled when Escape is pressed.
Shows the value as hexadecimal text when hexadecimal mode is on, otherwise leaves display to the standard control.
Closes the string dialog as cancelled when Escape is pressed.

rules.statement: Editing a value replaces its data with the confirmed new data and keeps its name and kind; the value stays selected.
When a typed hexadecimal number is too large to fit, the value is set to the largest allowed value; text that is not a hexadecimal number leaves the value unchanged.

tasks.outcome: Remove keys or values from a policy file, either leaving a deletion instruction for the machine or forgetting them entirely.

actions.what: Marks a value for deletion, or clears or purges a selected key, as the person chooses.
Removes a key with its contents, or one value, from the policy file without leaving a deletion mark.
Closes the delete dialog as cancelled when Escape is pressed.
Accepts the delete dialog when a choice is made and asks for a value name when deleting one value.
Enables the value name box only while the delete-one-value option is chosen.

rules.statement: Forgetting a key asks "Are you sure you want to remove this key and all its contents?" and, on Yes, removes the key, all its sub-keys, every value and every clearing mark from the file with no deletion left behind; No changes nothing. Forgetting a value removes the value and its deletion entry the same way.

Deleting a single value from the list does not erase it from the file: it is replaced by a deletion entry named "**del." followed by the value name, which removes the value on the machine when policies are applied.
The value name box in the delete dialog can be typed in only while the option to delete one value is chosen.

When Delete is confirmed with the option to clear the key or to delete all values under it, the choice is accepted without further input; no option is chosen when the dialog opens, and confirming with none chosen does nothing.

Deleting a key offers three choices, and OK does nothing until one is chosen; cancelling or Escape changes nothing. Clear everything removes all values and marks the key cleared. Clear first marks the key cleared and puts back only its existing direct values with ordinary content; deletion entries already in that key are lost and values of sub-keys are not put back. Delete one value is refused with "You must enter a value name." when the name is empty; otherwise any value of that name, whether or not it exists, is removed and replaced by a deletion entry.
When Delete is confirmed with the option to delete one value and the value name is empty, it is refused and the person is told "You must enter a value name."; with a name, the choice is accepted.

tasks.outcome: Bring the contents of an exported set of machine settings into a policy source.

actions.what: Loads the chosen REG file with its prefix and applies it to the policy source.
Closes the window as cancelled when Escape is pressed.
Opens the registry file import dialog and refreshes the list if values were imported.
Imports a registry export (REG) file into a policy source.
Lets the person pick a REG file and guesses the key prefix from it.

rules.statement: Only files of type *.reg are offered by the file chooser when browsing for the REG file.
When the guess fails, the person is only warned "An error occurred while trying to guess the prefix." and the prefix stays empty.
A REG key name is shortened by the prefix only when it starts with it, regardless of case. A prefix always ends in a backslash.
A REG file is reported as holding default values when any value has an empty name.
A REG file value line starting with an at sign is the key's default value, with an empty name.

When a REG file is applied to a source, a key marked for removal is cleared, a value marked for deletion is deleted and any other value is saved. A key name starting with the prefix is applied without it. A key not starting with the prefix is applied with its full original name, so the registry source would create a key of that name. The source branch limit is not checked.
A REG file is refused when its first line is not 'Windows Registry Editor Version 5.00', with the message 'Incorrect REG signature'.
Blank lines and lines starting with a semicolon in a REG file are ignored.
A REG key header starting with a minus sign marks the whole key for removal. Otherwise it opens a key whose values follow.
Pressing Escape closes Import REG as cancelled.

In a REG file, a value written as a bare minus sign is a value to delete. A quoted value is text, 'dword:' is a 32-bit number in hexadecimal, and 'hex' is bytes, typed by the number in brackets or binary if none. Data in none of these forms is kept as a value with no data and no type, with no error, and applying it writes an empty value or fails.
Importing a registry file (REG) applies it to the policy source of the area the person chooses and refreshes the view.
Import loads the REG file with the prefix and applies it straight to the chosen policy source; on any failure the person is told only "Failed to import the REG file."

The prefix of a REG file is guessed from its first key only. For a key starting with 'HKEY_USERS\' it is that hive plus the user identifier. For any other key, including HKEY_CURRENT_USER, it is the hive name alone. A first key with no further backslash gives an empty prefix. A file with no keys gets 'HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\'.

When a REG file is chosen and the prefix is empty, the prefix is guessed from the file; if the file holds default values, the person is warned "This REG file contains data for default values, which cannot be applied to all policy sources."
Import is refused with "Please specify a REG file to import." when no file is named, and with "Please specify the prefix used to fully qualify paths in the REG file." when no prefix is given.

tasks.outcome: Load a policy file into the user or computer policy source.

actions.what: Reads a chosen POL file and applies it to the user or computer policy source.

rules.statement: Importing a POL file applies it to the source the person chooses (user or computer). A file that cannot be read gives "The POL file could not be loaded." and changes nothing; success gives "POL import successful.". Nothing reaches disk until the person saves.
Applying a whole policy file to a source applies it as the difference from an empty file, so nothing is forgotten.

tasks.outcome: Write a policy source, or one branch of it, as an exported set of machine settings.

actions.what: Opens the registry file export dialog for the selected key.
Exports a policy source as a registry export (REG) file.
Closes the dialog as cancelled when Escape is pressed
Writes the chosen branch of the policy file to a .reg file
Lets the person pick the .reg file to write

rules.statement: The registry prefix box in the export dialog starts as HKEY_CURRENT_USER\ when the user policy source is being edited and HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\ otherwise. It can be changed, and the export uses the text in the box unchecked.
When the registry script is written, the person is told "REG exported successfully." and the dialog closes; on any failure they are told only "Failed to export REG!" and the dialog stays open.

Exporting to a registry file (REG) hands the policy source of the area the person chooses, as a POL, to the export dialog. An unsupported source raises an unhandled error, unlike Export POL, which tells the person.
A branch name given as the source of a REG export has any trailing backslash removed.

When a POL is built from a registry-backed source, every value and every sub-key under each of the three policy locations is copied with its own data type, with environment variables left unexpanded. A location missing from the registry stops the copy with an unhandled error.
Keys marked for removal are written to a REG file with a leading minus sign and values marked for deletion as a bare minus sign.

The export dialog starts with the selected key as its source branch, or empty when nothing is selected. The branch can be typed over, and the export uses the text in the box at the time: an empty box exports all of the policy file.

Exporting uses a source backed by a POL file as is. A registry-backed source (a chosen registry key or a loaded user hive file) is rebuilt as a new POL from the three policy locations: software\policies, software\microsoft\windows\currentversion\policies and system\currentcontrolset\policies. Any other source type is rejected, which no known source type reaches.

When a REG file is written, a default value is shown as an at sign, and quotes and backslashes in names and text are escaped. Text is written as quoted text and a 32-bit number as 'dword:' with eight hexadecimal digits. Every other type, including 64-bit numbers, expandable text and multiple strings, is written as hex bytes. Each carries its type number as hex(n), except plain binary, which is written as hex. Lines wrap before column 78 with a trailing backslash.
Export to a registry script is refused until a file name is given; the person is told "Please specify a filename and path for the exported REG."

Lets the person pick a folder in a folder dialog and puts it in the folder box.
Takes the chosen folder, checks it exists and closes the window with OK.
Looks for the domain's SYSVOL policy definitions folder and enables that choice only if it exists.
Closes the window as cancelled when Escape is pressed.

When opening a definitions folder fails, the person is told "The folder could not be fully added to the workspace." with the reason. The workspace may already be emptied or partly filled, the remembered folder is unchanged, and the view is rebuilt anyway.
The option to clear the workspace before adding the folder is ticked by default, and its choice is passed on only when a folder that exists was accepted.

When OK is pressed in the ADMX folder dialog, the folder is the system's Windows PolicyDefinitions folder, the domain SYSVOL folder, or the typed folder, as chosen. A folder that does not exist is refused with "The folder you specified does not exist." and the dialog stays open.

A definitions folder is remembered as the definitions folder for the next start only when "clear workspace" was chosen and the load did not fail; when the workspace is added to, the remembered folder is unchanged.

When the ADMX folder dialog opens, 'This folder' is chosen first, and the 'The domain's SYSVOL' choice is available only if the computer is joined to a domain and the folder \\domain\SYSVOL\domain\Policies\PolicyDefinitions exists.
The folder box and its Browse button are usable only when the 'This folder' choice is selected.
Pressing Escape closes the ADMX folder dialog as cancelled, with no folder chosen.
